newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Bank Negara says capital curbs a possible option.
newsitem.headline: Bank Negara says capital curbs a possible option.

text.p: Malaysia may consider capital controls as one possible option if short-term capital inflows played too dominant a role in the banking system, Bank Negara Assistant Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz was quoted as saying in Hong Kong on Monday.
At present balance sheets of Malaysian banks are heavily skewed towards short-term capital, research firm I.D.E.A. quoted her as saying at a conference sponsored by I.D.E.A in Hong Kong.
"Bank Negara Malaysia would act pro-actively if it felt that short-term capital was playing too dominant a role in overall fund inflows into the country," I.D.E.A. said quoting Zeti.
She said that Asian central banks had three policy options to confront capital inflows -- allowing currency appreciation, increasing forex reserves and imposing capital controls.
"Zeti said that BNM favours the use of all three options," the I.D.E.A report said.
She however said that Bank Negara would intervene in the foreign exchange market only if dollar/ringgit moved in divergence to the country's changing economic fundamentals.

Bank Negara last imposed capital controls in early 1994. To curb what it said was "hot money" flowing into the country, it banned the sale of government paper to foreigners and imposed negative interest rates on foreign-held ringgit accounts, among other measures.
The funds were attracted by the sharply higher interest rates in Malaysia, a situation similar to that prevalent now, analysts said.

Higher yields have this year attracted a large amount of short-term funds, but volumes have been sharply lower than in 1994 mainly due to similarly higher interest rates in other countries of the region, they said.
